<div class="game-page">

<div class="game-meta">game</div>
<div class="game-subtitle">(The 1790 edition prints this as the Sixth Regular Party.)</div>
<hr class="game-rule">
<div class="editorial-note"><strong>Editorial note.</strong> The editions disagree at Black&#x27;s 4th move. 1777 reads &quot;the queen&#x27;s pawn, one move&quot; (d6), as transcribed here; 1790 reads &quot;two moves&quot; (d5), which is also the reading in modern transcriptions of this game and the move the following play assumes. Treat 1777 as a misprint.</div>
<div class="editorial-note"><strong>Reconstructed 🐞.</strong> The board plays the game through. The printed text admits no legal continuation at ply 8, 10, so the board departs from it there. Philidor's words stand unaltered beside it.</div>
</div>
<div class="philidor-game">
<div class="game-board">
<div class="pgn-board"><script type="text/pgn">[Event "Philidor, Analysis of the Game of Chess (London, 1777)"]
[Site "?"]
[Date "1777.??.??"]
[Round "-"]
[White "Philidor (analysis)"]
[Black "Philidor (analysis)"]
[Result "*"]
[Annotator "F. D. Philidor"]
[PhilidorGame "Another Method of Playing"]
[PhilidorKind "game"]
[SourceLine "7058"]
[PhilidorReconstructed "Completing this game meant reading against the text at ply 8, 10; the printed reading admits no legal continuation."]

1. e4 {The king's pawn, two moves.} c5 {The queen's bishop's pawn, two moves. (a) NOTE: This way
of opening the game, when you have not the move, is absolutely defensive, and very far from
being the best, especially if some advantage is granted: but it is a very good one to try the
strength of an adversary with whose skill you are unacquainted.} 2. f4 {The king's bishop's
pawn, two moves.} Nc6 {The queen's knight, at his bishop's third square.} 3. Nf3 {The king's
knight, at his bishop's third square. (b) NOTE: On this move, he might have forced you to play
the gambit, by pushing his king's pawn two moves; and you could not have taken, without being
exposed to a check from his queen; and he would have won the game.} e6 {The king's pawn, one
move.} 4. c3 {The queen's bishop's pawn, one move. (c) NOTE: You might have pushed your queen's
pawn two moves, in order to change it with his queen's bishop's pawn. This move may be played
so, and not badly: but, in that case, you must preserve your queen's bishop, to oppose, in case
of need, to his royal bishop, who, placed at his queen's bishop's fourth square, might hinder
you from castling on your right side, and be besides very troublesome to all your pieces.} f6
{The queen's pawn, one move.} 5. e5 {The king's pawn, one move.} d5 {The king's bishop's pawn,
two moves. (d) NOTE: Instead of this move, he might have played his queen's pawn one move. In
that case, you must have taken his pawn with yours, to hinder him from settling the same
position on the side of his queen, who is now standing on your king's side.} 6. d4 {The queen's
pawn, two moves.} Nh6 {The king's knight, at his rook's third square. (e) NOTE: The taking of
your queen's bishop, opening the way for the getting out of his queen's knight, would be very
bad play on his part; as it would be for you to take his pawn with yours, which would give an
advantageous place to his king's bishop.} 7. Be3 {The queen's bishop, at his king's third
square.} Qb6 {The queen, at her knight's third square. (f) NOTE: He attacks your queen's
knight's pawn, with a design to induce you to push it again one move: but it is better to
sustain it, because, in case you advance it, he might, by pushing his queen's rook's pawn two
moves, form a very successful attack on your left wing.} 8. Qd2 {The queen, at her second
square.} Nf7 {The king's knight, at his bishop's second square. (g) NOTE: Had he attacked your
queen's bishop with this knight, you must not then have given him leave to change piece for
piece: you should, in that case, have withdrawn your bishop, and afterwards forced his knight to
retreat.} 9. dxc5 {The queen's pawn takes the bishop's pawn. (h). NOTE: As your queen's knight
cannot get out, without exposing you to the risk of having either a pawn doubled, or your queen
forced, it is necessary to get rid of his king's bishop.} Bxc5 {The king's bishop retakes the
pawn.} 10. Bxc5 {The queen's bishop takes the bishop.} Qxc5 {The queen retakes the bishop.} 11.
Na3 {The queen's knight, at his rook's third square. (i) NOTE: You play this knight, to the end
that he may re-unite your royal knight at your queen's fourth square. It is the best place he
can take in the present situation. In general, when one has two knights, it is very material to
open between them a reciprocal communication, and post them on such squares, where they can be
neither attacked by the pawns, nor forced to retreat.} g5 {The king's knight's pawn, two moves.
(k) NOTE: He pushes this pawn with a view to break your centre; and it would be very bad play in
you to take his pawn.} 12. g3 {The king's knight's pawn, one move.} h5 {The king's rook's pawn,
two moves. (l) NOTE: He pushes this pawn, with a design to make an opening for his king's rook;
and, were you to give him time for pushing it still one move, he could force and break backwards
the chain of your pawns.} 13. h4 {The king's rook's pawn, two moves.} gxh4 {The king's knight's
pawn takes the bishop's pawn. (m) NOTE: As your king's knight, being sustained by two pawns, may
safely place himself at his fifth square, your adversary takes your pawn, to procure likewise to
his king's knight such a post.} 14. gxh4 {The king's knight's pawn retakes the pawn.} Rg8 {The
king's rook, at its knight's square. (n) NOTE: He plays this rook to secure the command of all
the line. Here is an example where a rook may well be sacrificed for another piece. I suppose
that you don't close that line with your knight; he would then remove to your king's knight's
fourth square his rook, which, supported and sustained by two pawns, could not be taken without
re-uniting his pawns.} 15. Ng5 {The king's knight, at his fifth square.} Nh6 {The king's knight,
at his rook's third square. (o) NOTE: He plays this knight with a design to procure him as good
a place as yours now occupies.} 16. Nc2 {The queen's knight, at his bishop's second square.} Ng4
{The king's knight, at his fifth square.} 17. Nd4 {The queen's knight, at his queen's fourth
square. (p) NOTE: You break by this move the direction of his queen, and your two knights are
now re-united to attack and take his king's pawn.} Ke7 {The king, at his second square.} 18. Be2
{The king's bishop, at his king's second square.} Bd7 {The queen's bishop, at his queen's second
square.} 19. O-O {The king castles with his rook. (q) NOTE: It would be very dangerous to castle
on your left, because he might very easily form his attack upon your king. In that position,
besides, your king must occupy his knight's third square, in order to keep in the adverse king's
knight, and in the mean while sustain your pawns.} Rac8 {The queen's rook, at its bishop's
square. 20.} 20. Rac1 {The queen's rook, at its bishop's square. (r) NOTE: This move is
absolutely necessary, to hinder him from making himself master of that line, by changing his
knight with your's. By this position alone he would undoubtedly win the game. You must always
oppose your rooks to the adversary's rooks, and never give up the openings to him. In this
situation the game is almost even: nevertheless, as there is a pawn advanced on the ground of
the black, some fort of advantage lies on the side of the white.} *
</script></div>
